sentences.text: This pterosaur had a wingspan of about 4 meters and weighed approximately 10 kilograms.
Its skull was estimated to be about 60 centimeters long.
A unique premaxillary crest rose at a 60-degree angle to a rounded top, with a base length of 131 millimeters and a height of 128 millimeters.
This crest was very thin transversely, measuring only up to 4 millimeters in thickness.
The animal possessed a total of fifty teeth in its head, with twelve in the upper jaw and thirteen in the lower jaw.
The first tooth pair in the snout and lower jaws was smaller than the other front teeth, and the first pair in the premaxillae pointed vertically.
The fossil consists of a partial skeleton including the skull and lower jaws, largely preserved in three dimensions due to the ironstone, though some bones have been crushed.
The specimen represents a fully developed but immature animal.
A sharp, 60-degree angled crest on the snout is a striking feature of this species.
The name Ferrodraco combines Latin words for 'iron' and 'dragon' because the skeleton was found in ironstone.
The specific name honors Graham Thomas 'Butch' Lenton, the late mayor of Winton Shire, for his community work and support of the Australian Age of Dinosaurs.
The holotype was discovered in April 2017 by cattle farmer Robert A. Elliott while spraying herbicide near the Belmont station.
The species Ferrodraco lentoni was named and described in 2019 by a team led by Adele H. Pentland, including Stephen Francis Poropat, Travis R. Tischler, Trish Sloan, and the Elliott family.
The first tooth pair in the snout and lower jaws was smaller than the other front teeth, and the first pair in the premaxillae pointed vertically.
Ferrodraco is classified in the class Reptilia.

One analysis placed it within the clade Ornithocheirae as the sister species to Mythunga, while a more recent 2020 study by Borja Holgado and Rodrigo Pêgas placed it within the family Anhangueridae, specifically in the subfamily Tropeognathinae, though it remains the sister taxon to Mythunga.
Researchers suggest that the exact position of Ferrodraco within Anhangueridae remains uncertain.

The holotype was found in the Winton Formation dating to the lower Cenomanian-Turonian, approximately 96 million years ago, and the animal lived from the Cenomanian to the Turonian, between 100.5 and 89.8 million years ago.

It is debated whether a 2010 report of an ornithocheirid jaw fragment from Australia represents a younger species, as the Molecap Greensand layers where it was found may date to a time younger than Ferrodraco.
